newsitem.title: USA: NYC economy slowed in Q3 to 1.6 pct rise -- official.
newsitem.headline: NYC economy slowed in Q3 to 1.6 pct rise -- official.

text.p: New York City's economy slowed during the third quarter, with the gross city product rising only at a 1.6 percent annual rate, when adjusted for inflation, the city comptroller said Wednesday.
Weakness in retail sales and at least a brief slowdown in private sector hirings pulled the rate down from the 2.5 percent pace seen in the second quarter of 1996.

"There are a number of signs of weakness in the city's economy," Hevesi said, in prepared remarks. Retail sailes, on a year-over-year basis, grew only 2.9 percent in the first two months of the third quarter.
That was down from the 4.1 percent rise seen in retail sales during the first half of the year.

The private sector, which created an average of 4,717 jobs a month in the first six months of the year, has only generated 1,133 jobs a month since June. However, saying the slowdown might be temporary, the comptroller added that the city's workforce grew by 5,000 jobs in September, rebounding from the July's drop of 3,800, and August's decline of 500.
Hevesi highlighted the problems posed by the state's deregulation of hospital reimbursement rates and reductions in spending on health care.

Predicting that job losses in health care and social services will grow, Hevesi said, "This creates a problem for New York City, since health care and social services have been the main source of new jobs, especially entry-level jobs."

Still, the comptroller noted that the hotel industry "remained vibrant," with the occupancy rate climbing to 82.7 percent, up from 80.1 percent a year-ago. Guests paid a daily rate of $160.70, a $17.60 rise.
And the Manhattan office market improved, with leasing rising by 75,651 square feet to 20 million square feet over a year ago, despite a drop in Midtown South.
Overall vacancy rates in Manhattan fell to 14 percent from 14.7 percent a year-ago. However, asking rental rates for Class A properties slipped to $33.73, down 28 cents from the 1995 third quarter.
Other highlights of the comptroller's report follow.
--Jobs in the city rose by 2,100 in the third quarter, against the second quarter's 12,200 rise, when data are seasonally adjusted.

--Business services gained 4,100 jobs, with entertainment adding 1,600. Health services, which last lost jobs in the 1986 fourth quarter, shed 500, with social services, which until the second quarter had added jobs for 34 consectutive quarters, dropped again, losing 300 positions.
--The number of city residents with jobs rose by 7,600 in the third quarter to a seasonally adjusted 2.946 million. The second-quarter rise was 8,800.
--New York area inflation was unchanged at 2.8 percent, level with a year-ago.

--Except for the help-wanted advertisement index, leading economic indicators showed slower gains. The total number of building permits authorized grew by 682 in the third quarter, down from 2,403 in the second quarter. Intial jobless claims rose to 35,083 a month, up from 33,373 in the second quarter.
But the help-wanted advertisement index rose to 51 in the third quarter from 48.3 in the second quarter.

--Personal income climbed due to rising capital gains, interest income and dividends. Quarterly estimated payments jumped 23.4 percent in the third quarter, against the year-ago period's 0.6 percent drop. Wages witheld rose 7.4 percent against the year-ago's 3.8 percent level.

--Yet hourly earnings were lackluster. In the durable goods sector, they rose 3.6 percent, the biggest third quarter rise. Still, retail workers were hit by a 1.2 percent drop to $9 an hour from the year-ago level.
--Joan Gralla, 212-859-1654
